stories.title: The group chat is loud.
stories.speaker: wolf
stories.body: Everyone is talking about Aster. “It’s going up,” says Wolf. The screenshot has no source. Your coffee isn’t even cold yet.

choices.label: Ask for the source
choices.outcome: Wolf sends the original post. It is three months old. You put the excitement on pause and open the company update.
choices.takeaway: A screenshot is a starting point, not the whole story.

choices.label: Watch for a while
choices.outcome: You leave Aster on your watchlist. Later, the chat gets quiet. You kept your options open without making a trade.
choices.takeaway: Waiting is a decision too.

choices.label: Follow the crowd
choices.outcome: In this story, you rush in. A second message contradicts the first. Now you have a position, but no reason you trust.
choices.takeaway: Before following a crowd, write down what would change your mind.

stories.title: A red morning.
stories.speaker: sal
stories.body: Aster is down 6% in this desk story. Sal drops a note beside your screen: “Price moved. What else changed?”

choices.label: Read the company update
choices.outcome: Revenue is steady, but costs rose. You now have a fact to compare with your original plan.
choices.takeaway: Price and business performance are different pieces of evidence.

choices.label: Open my original plan
choices.outcome: Your note says you would review after the next results. You set the headline beside that plan before making a new call.
choices.takeaway: A plan gives you something to revisit when emotions get loud.

choices.label: Sell because it is red
choices.outcome: You react to the colour before reading the update. The story pauses there; selling may fit a plan, but red alone does not explain one.
choices.takeaway: Ask what changed before choosing your response.

stories.title: One very big position.
stories.speaker: oracle
stories.body: One company now makes up 70% of your fictional desk. Oracle turns the monitor towards you: “A good week made this desk very lopsided.”

choices.label: Look at the whole desk
choices.outcome: You compare how much depends on this one company. A small move there could now dominate everything else.
choices.takeaway: Look at position size as well as performance.

choices.label: Consider trimming it
choices.outcome: You work through a smaller position on paper before acting. You are deciding how much uncertainty to carry.
choices.takeaway: Reducing concentration is a risk decision, not a prediction.

choices.label: Leave it for now
choices.outcome: You keep the position, and write down why you are comfortable with the concentration. You also choose when to review it.
choices.takeaway: Keeping a position still deserves a deliberate reason.

stories.title: “That share is cheaper.”
stories.speaker: shark
stories.body: Shark points at two fictional companies: one share costs 5, the other 100. “Five is a bargain, right?”

choices.label: Ask how many shares exist
choices.outcome: The 5-priced company has far more shares. Share price alone did not tell you which whole business was cheaper.
choices.takeaway: Price per share and the value of a company are different.

choices.label: Look at the businesses
choices.outcome: You put earnings, debt and expectations beside the price. There is more work to do before calling either a bargain.
choices.takeaway: A low share price is not an investment case.

choices.label: Pick the lower number
choices.outcome: The low price catches your eye. Sal slides over the share counts; that single number was missing most of the comparison.
choices.takeaway: The smallest number is not automatically the best value.

stories.title: Before you close the laptop.
stories.speaker: sal
stories.body: It has been a noisy week. Sal leaves one empty note on your desk. You have time for one useful thing.

choices.label: Review one decision
choices.outcome: You compare your reason with what happened. A good result can follow a weak process, and a careful decision can still lose.
choices.takeaway: Review the reasoning as well as the result.

choices.label: Write next week’s plan
choices.outcome: You note one company to research and one question you still cannot answer. Monday now has a starting point.
choices.takeaway: An unanswered question can be a useful next step.

choices.label: Take the evening off
choices.outcome: You close the desk without forcing one more trade. The market will still be there when you return.
choices.takeaway: You do not need a trade for every visit.

stories.title: Same company. Different token.
stories.speaker: oracle
stories.body: Two tokens follow the same company. Their names look familiar. Oracle puts their issuer pages side by side.

choices.label: Read the issuer terms
choices.outcome: The pages describe different rights and redemption routes. You check the token itself, not just the company name.
choices.takeaway: A token linked to a share does not automatically give you every shareholder right.

choices.label: Compare the markets
choices.outcome: You notice different liquidity and prices. You add issuer terms to your checks before treating them as interchangeable.
choices.takeaway: Company identity, token terms and trading conditions all matter.

choices.label: Trust the matching logo
choices.outcome: The logos match, but the contracts and terms do not. You stop before assuming that the pictures prove equivalence.
choices.takeaway: A familiar logo does not verify an asset.

stories.title: A quieter desk.
stories.speaker: sal
stories.body: No rush today. Sal asks you to pick one thing you want to understand better before the next busy day.

choices.label: How one company makes money
choices.outcome: You make a short list: who pays, what they buy, and what it costs to deliver. You have a research plan for your next visit.
choices.takeaway: Start with the business behind the symbol.

choices.label: What could go wrong
choices.outcome: You name one assumption in your plan and what evidence would challenge it. Uncertainty is easier to discuss when it is specific.
choices.takeaway: A risk is more useful when you can explain it.

choices.label: What I changed my mind about
choices.outcome: You reread an old reason and add what you see differently now. Changing your mind can be part of a careful process.
choices.takeaway: Keep a record of how your thinking changes.
